name: Interview brainteasers, set 1
description: Brainteasers of the kind interviewers ask: crossings, ropes, clocks, jugs, eggs, hats, pirates, weighings, parity and trailing zeros. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Five people cross a bridge at night with one torch. They take 1, 3, 4, 9 and 11 minutes. At most two cross at once, at the slower one's pace, and the torch goes with every crossing.
items.question: What is the shortest total time, in minutes?

widget.accept: 26: the 1 and 3 shuttle the torch for the 9 and 11, then the 1 walks the 4.
widget.label: Total minutes

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the fastest escorting with the slow pair crossing together.

byKey.escort: You had the fastest walk everyone over. Sending the 9 and the 11 together saves their slower times.
byKey.sum: You added every crossing time once. Someone must also bring the torch back each time.

explain.text: The 1 and 3 cross, the 1 returns, the 9 and 11 cross and the 3 returns: $3 + 1 + 11 + 3 = 18$. Then the 1 and 3 cross, the 1 returns and the 1 and 4 cross: $3 + 1 + 4 = 8$. That totals 26, against 30 if the 1 walks everyone over.

items.prose: You have two ropes and a lighter. Each rope takes exactly 60 minutes to burn, but unevenly: half its length need not take half the time.
items.question: How do you measure exactly 45 minutes?

options.text: Light A at both ends and B at one end. When A goes out, light B's other end and wait for B.
Light A at both ends. When it goes out, light B at both ends, and stop when B goes out.
options.why: You lit B only after A went out, so that measures 30 + 30 = 60 minutes. B must already have burned for 30 minutes when its second end is lit.

options.text: Cut rope B at three quarters of its length, then burn the longer piece from one end.
options.why: You trusted the length, but the rope burns unevenly. Three quarters of its length need not take 45 minutes.

options.text: Light both ropes at both ends at the same moment, and stop when the second one goes out.
options.why: You lit everything at once, so both ropes go out together at 30 minutes. This measures only 30.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lighting a rope at both ends halves the time it has left.

explain.text: Rope A lit at both ends lasts 30 minutes, while B burns 30 minutes of its time from one end. B then has 30 minutes left, and lighting its other end halves that to 15. So B goes out at 30 + 15 = 45 minutes.

items.question: What is the smaller angle between the hands, in degrees?

widget.accept: 78°: the hour hand at 222°, the minute hand at 144°.
widget.label: Angle in degrees

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place each hand in degrees from 12, then subtract.

byKey.still-hour: You left the hour hand on the 7. In 24 minutes it moves on 12°, to 222°.
byKey.reflex: You gave the larger angle. The smaller one is 360 − 282 = 78°.

explain.text: The minute hand is at 24 × 6 = 144°. The hour hand is at 7 × 30 + 24 × 0.5 = 222°. The gap is 222 − 144 = 78°.

items.prose: You have a tap, a drain, a 9-litre jug and a 5-litre jug, neither marked. A step fills a jug, empties a jug, or pours one into the other. A pour stops when one jug is full or the other is empty.
items.question: What is the fewest steps that leaves exactly 3 litres in a jug?

widget.accept: 8 steps, starting by filling the 9-litre jug.
widget.label: Fewest steps

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each state as (9-litre, 5-litre) and search from (0, 0).

byKey.pours-only: You counted only the pours from jug to jug. Each fill and each empty is a step too.
byKey.five-first: That route starts by filling the 5-litre jug. Starting with the 9 reaches 3 litres two steps sooner.

explain.text: Fill the 9 and pour into the 5, leaving 4; empty the 5 and pour the 4 across. Fill the 9 again and top up the 5, leaving 8; empty the 5 and pour again, leaving 3. That is 8 steps, and a search of every state finds none shorter.

items.prose: You have two identical eggs and a 60-floor building. An egg breaks when dropped from some floor or higher, and survives below it. Find the highest safe floor, which may be none or the top.
items.question: What is the fewest drops that always finds it?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn it round: how many floors can d drops settle?

byKey.ten: Ten drops cover only 10 + 9 + ⋯ + 1 = 55 floors, short of 60.
byKey.binary: Halving the floors needs many eggs. With two, a break early leaves one egg to walk up floor by floor.

explain.text: With d drops the first egg leaps d floors, then d − 1, and so on. That covers 1 + 2 + ⋯ + d = d(d + 1)/2 floors. 10 drops cover 55, short of 60, and 11 cover 66.

items.prose: Seven prisoners stand in a line, each in a red or blue hat chosen by a fair coin. Each sees every hat in front, not their own. From the back, each calls a colour aloud. They agree a code first.
items.question: With the best code, how many do you expect to call their own colour? Give one decimal place.

widget.accept: 6.5: six always right, the back prisoner half the time.
widget.label: Expected number right

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the back prisoner's call can tell the others.

byKey.guaranteed: Six is what the code guarantees. The back prisoner is also right half the time, which adds 0.5.
byKey.coin: You treated every call as a coin flip. A parity call lets six prisoners deduce their own hat.
byKey.all: The back prisoner sees nothing that tells him his own hat. He is right only half the time.

explain.text: The back prisoner calls the parity of the reds ahead, so the six in front can deduce their hats. He learns nothing about his own hat, so he is right with chance 1/2. That gives 6 + 0.5 = 6.5 on average.

items.prose: Four pirates, A to D from the most senior, share 100 coins. The most senior alive proposes a split and all alive vote. A plan needs more than half the votes, or the proposer goes overboard. Each wants to survive, then coins, then to see others go overboard.
items.question: How many coins does A keep?

widget.accept: 98: A gives one coin each to C and D.
widget.label: Coins A keeps

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from two pirates and work back up.

byKey.half-rule: You let a tie pass. Here a plan needs more than half, so A needs three votes, not two.
byKey.three-bought: You paid B as well. B keeps all 100 if A goes, so no offer wins his vote.

explain.text: With C and D alone, C cannot win D's vote, so C would go overboard. So B wins C's vote with nothing and keeps all 100. A needs three votes, so he buys C and D with one coin each and keeps 98.

items.prose: Among 40 coins that look alike, one is heavier than the rest. You have a balance scale and nothing else.
items.question: What is the fewest weighings that always finds the heavy coin, and a first weighing that keeps that guarantee?

options.text: 4 weighings: first weigh 14 against 14, with 12 aside.
3 weighings: first weigh 14 against 14, with 12 aside.
options.why: You allowed three weighings, but they tell apart at most 3³ = 27 coins, and 40 is more.

options.text: 4 weighings: first weigh 5 against 5, with 30 aside.
options.why: If the heavy coin is among the 30 aside, three more weighings settle only 27 of them.

options.text: 6 weighings: halve the coins each time.
options.why: Halving uses only two outcomes. Each weighing has three: left heavy, right heavy, or level.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the outcomes of each weighing.

explain.text: Each weighing has three outcomes, so k weighings separate at most 3ᵏ coins. Since 27 < 40 ≤ 81, four are needed. After 14 against 14, every group left has at most 27 coins, which three more weighings settle.

items.prose: Ten lamps stand in a row, all off. A move switches over any three neighbouring lamps: those on go off and those off go on.
items.question: Can you reach all ten lamps on?

options.text: No. The seven lamps outside places 3, 6 and 9 always have an even number lit.
Yes. Switch lamps 1 to 3, then 4 to 6, then 7 to 9, and last of all 8 to 10.
options.why: You missed that the last move turns 8 and 9 off again. You end with lamps 8 and 9 off.

options.text: No. Each move changes the lit count by 1 or 3, an odd amount, and 10 is even.
options.why: You tracked one move only. Two moves change the count by an even amount, so this rules nothing out. You need a quantity that never changes.

options.text: Yes. With enough moves in the right order, any pattern can be reached from all off.
options.why: You assumed every pattern is reachable. A quantity that never changes shows all ten on is not.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a set of lamps whose lit count keeps its parity.

explain.text: Every three neighbours include exactly one of places 3, 6 and 9. So a move switches two of the other seven lamps, and their lit count stays even. All ten on would need all seven of them lit, an odd number.

items.prose: $250!$ is the product of the whole numbers from 1 to 250.
items.question: How many zeros does $250!$ end in?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the factors of 5 in the product.

byKey.fives-only: You counted multiples of 5 once each. Multiples of 25 and 125 hold extra fives.
byKey.no-125: You missed 125 and 250, which each hold a third five.
byKey.tens: You counted multiples of 10. Every 5 pairs with one of the many 2s, so count the 5s.

explain.text: Each trailing zero needs a factor 2 × 5, and 2s are plentiful, so count the 5s. Multiples of 5, 25 and 125 give 50 + 10 + 2 = 62. So $250!$ ends in 62 zeros.
